oldEvidenceRetained.quote: The Kiger Laboratory @ UCSD

Our laboratory is studying central roles for novel membrane trafficking processes, under control of spatiotemporal lipid regulation, that coordinate dynamic cell structure. Using a foundation in genetic and cell biology experiments in the fruit fly, Drosophila, we are linking specific lipid kinase and phosphatase activities to cell remodeling.

Our research is currently focused in three major areas: (1) roles for phosphoinositide lipid regulation in cellular remodeling, (2) roles for autophagy in cellular remodeling, and (3) systems-biology approaches to understand cellular remodeling.
To address these problems, we are investigating questions specific to the dynamic organization of two distinct cell types, immune cells and muscle cells.

Why do we do the research?

Investigation of the development of neuronal excitability led to the discovery that calcium-dependent embryonic electrical activity rapidly and reversibly reconfigures the transmitters and matching postsynaptic transmitter receptors that neurons express.
Both sensory and motor stimuli reprogram neurotransmitter identity, resulting in transmitter switches in young and adult nervous systems.

The changes in brain biochemistry during transmitter switching cause changes in behavior that can be beneficial, enhancing learning, or detrimental, contributing to neurological and psychiatric disorders.
